title: Natural Gas Is the Next AI Bottleneck, and Investors Are Racing to Get Ahead of It
excerpt: As Big Tech pours hundreds of billions into AI data centers, a looming natural gas shortage could reshape the power landscape and create a new class of Wall Street winners.
body:
• Chronometer Partners warns that a U.S. natural gas supply deficit is unavoidable by the second half of 2028, driven by AI data center power demand and surging LNG exports.
  • Microsoft, Google, and Meta are all building massive natural gas power plants in the southern U.S. to feed their AI infrastructure, with Meta's Louisiana site alone reaching 7.46 GW of capacity.
  • Gas turbine prices are expected to rise 195% from 2019 levels, with new orders backed up until 2028 and six-year delivery timelines, according to Wood Mackenzie.
  • Upstream gas producers and nuclear infrastructure companies stand to benefit, while hyperscalers could see energy costs triple from 10% to 30% of total compute spending by 2029.

The AI industry has spent the last two years scrambling for chips. The next scramble, according to a growing chorus of energy analysts and investors, will be for something far more basic: natural gas.

The Supply Crunch Ahead

Matthew Smith, founder and CIO of investment firm Chronometer Partners, laid out the thesis on the Invest Like the Best podcast this week. After 18 months of research, his firm concluded that a U.S. natural gas shortage is effectively unavoidable by mid-2028.

"Natural gas, which represents over 40% of U.S. power generation, is imminently going to become the most important fuel in the country," Smith said. The U.S. currently produces 110-112 billion cubic feet (Bcf) per day and exports roughly 15 Bcf daily, with exports scheduled to reach 35 Bcf by 2030.

Even if production climbs to 132 Bcf — which Chronometer considers a ceiling — the math does not work. Smith projects a deficit exceeding 5 Bcf per day "before the full force of AI demand" hits, according to MarketWatch.

"Gas has lulled everybody to sleep, but what happens is these structural things start to fall into place in 2027-2028, and we start to draw down meaningfully in the middle of 2028."

— Matthew Smith, Founder and CIO, Chronometer Partners

Big Tech's Gas Rush

The tech industry's pivot to natural gas has accelerated dramatically. Microsoft announced a partnership with Chevron and Engine No. 1 to build a natural gas power plant in West Texas that could generate up to 5 GW. Google confirmed a deal with Crusoe for a 933 MW gas plant in North Texas. Meta added seven more gas plants to its Hyperion data center in Louisiana, bringing the site to 7.46 GW — enough to power the entire state of South Dakota, according to TechCrunch.

Oracle's Project Jupiter in New Mexico, meanwhile, will be fully powered by Bloom Energy fuel cells running on natural gas, replacing the gas turbines and diesel generators originally planned.

The rush has created its own bottleneck. Gas turbine prices are projected to surge 195% by end of 2026 relative to 2019 levels, according to Wood Mackenzie. Equipment contributes 20-30% of power plant construction costs, and new turbine orders cannot be placed until 2028, with delivery timelines stretching to six years.

Winners and Losers

For investors, the natural gas deficit thesis reshuffles the AI trade. Smith identified upstream producers as clear beneficiaries — companies like Expand Energy, which controls high-quality rock formations that allow faster, cheaper extraction, and Range Resources, which has room to grow production.

On the demand side, fuel cell maker Bloom Energy has seen its first-quarter revenue soar 130% year over year, while GE Vernova's gas turbine backlog grew from 83 GW to 100 GW in a single quarter. Bloom's CEO KR Sridhar told investors that on-site power has moved "from a decision of last resort to a vital business necessity."

But Smith warns the current AI infrastructure darlings could become casualties. As gas supply tightens, "orders for turbines and fuel cells could slow meaningfully." Hyperscalers face an even bleaker calculus: energy currently accounts for about 10% of compute costs, but if gas prices double or triple structurally, that figure could hit 20-30% by 2029.

The Nuclear Endgame

Smith's longer-term view points to nuclear as the only viable solution. As the gas deficit worsens into the early 2030s, "the only viable solution is to build large-scale nuclear as fast as possible, which would mean it needs to come on in 2033 or 2034," he said. Companies like Cameco and BWX Technologies, a primary supplier of nuclear hardware for the U.S. Navy, could benefit.

Goldman Sachs projects data centers will consume 8% of America's total electricity by 2030, with 60% of that powered by natural gas — adding emissions equivalent to 15.7 million additional cars on the road.

What to Watch

Natural gas prices remain down 8% in 2026, a lag Smith attributes to years of abundance masking structural tightening. For Indian-origin investors and tech professionals — many of whom hold significant positions in the AI sector — the energy equation adds a new variable to the bull case for Big Tech. The companies building the AI future may find their biggest constraint is not silicon, but fuel.
